content: The cyanate ion is an anion composed of one oxygen atom, one carbon atom, and one nitrogen atom, arranged in that specific order. It carries a single unit of negative charge, which is primarily localized on the nitrogen atom. In organic chemistry, the cyanate group functions as a functional group. The structure of the cyanate ion can be described as resonating between two canonical forms, resulting in a resonance hybrid. This hybrid structure can be represented as a combination of these two contributing forms. The cyanate ion is isoelectronic with carbon dioxide, meaning it has the same number of electrons and, as a result, shares a similar linear molecular geometry. In nucleophilic substitution reactions, the cyanate ion acts as an ambident nucleophile. This means it can react in two distinct ways: it can form an alkyl cyanate (R-OCN) or an alkyl isocyanate (R-NCO). The formation of alkyl isocyanates is generally the predominant pathway, while alkyl cyanates are exceptions. Aryl cyanates, such as phenyl cyanate (C6H5OCN), can be synthesized through the reaction of phenol with cyanogen chloride (ClCN) in the presence of a base. Cyanates are either salts or esters of cyanic acid. Examples include potassium cyanate (KOCN) and methyl cyanate. The cyanate ion is relatively non-toxic compared to cyanides. This property is utilized in cyanide decontamination processes, where toxic cyanide is oxidized by permanganate to produce the safer cyanate ion. It is important to note that the fulminate ion (CNO⁻) has the same chemical formula as the cyanate ion but differs in structure. The fulminate ion is a structural isomer of the cyanate ion.
